title: Short-Form Video Editing
subtitle: Hold the first two seconds, then make it repeatable
summary: Editing vertical video that people actually finish. Twelve lessons on the opening seconds, pace and cutting, the on-screen text and sound that have to carry a video watched with the volume down, and a production routine that turns a batch of videos into an afternoon instead of a week. Shot on a phone, edited on a phone or a laptop, and taught as principles rather than a tour of one app's menus.
description: This course is for Filipino freelancers, VAs, students and jobseekers who are already handed footage, or who film on their own phone, and need the edit to be the part that earns money. You will learn what the opening frame and the first spoken line have to do before a thumb moves, how to shoot so there is something to cut, how to strip dead air and then build a pace that varies instead of one that just runs fast, when a word on screen does work no shot can do, how to caption for a viewer with the sound off in a jeep, how to keep voice and music from fighting each other, and how to set up a project, a template and a review pass so ten videos come out of one sitting at a quality you can defend. Every technique is described in terms any editor on any app can carry out, because the app you use this year is not the app you will use next year. The course does not teach you to sell the service, price it, or run the client's account: it teaches you to make the video.

Run a batch of videos through one setup, one template and one review pass in a single sitting

lessons.title: The first two seconds
lessons.content_mdx:
# The first two seconds

The opening of a short video is not a title card. It is an offer: stay, and here is what you get. If the offer is not on screen straight away, nothing you built after it will ever be seen.

Mariel edits for a milk tea shop in Bacolod. Her first cut opened with the shop logo spinning in, then the owner saying "Hi guys, welcome back." The drink does not appear until the video is a third over. No single part of that is a mistake. Together they ask the viewer to wait, and a thumb does not wait.

## Three things arrive at once

**The first frame.** What is on screen the instant the video starts, before anyone has heard a word.

**The first words.** The first thing the voice says, or the first line of text if there is no voice.

**The first movement.** Something changing: a hand entering frame, a cut, the subject turning, a lid coming off.

All three land together and all three have to work. A strong first line over a static empty counter is still a weak opening. So is a good-looking moving shot over a line that says nothing.

## What the viewer is deciding

Nobody consciously decides to watch. They glance and answer three questions without noticing:

- Is there a person, or is something happening?
- Can I tell what this is about?
- Is it about me?

If the answers are not yes right away, they scroll. They are not rejecting your edit. They never got far enough to have an opinion about it.

## Four openings that lose

**The logo intro.** Branding at the top is for the client's pride. Put it on the last frame, where it lands on people who stayed.

**The greeting.** "Hi guys, welcome back po." A greeting is what you say to someone who has already sat down. Your viewer has not sat down.

**The wide establishing shot.** A wide of a room tells the viewer about the room. Vertical video is a narrow frame held at arm's length, so a wide shot puts a small subject in a lot of empty space. Start closer than feels comfortable.

**The line that describes the video.** "Today I am going to show you how we pack an order." That is a table of contents, and nobody came for the table of contents. "We used to lose one order a week to this" is a start.

## Four moves that work

**Start on the strongest frame you have, not the first one you shot.** Scrub the footage. Find the moment with the best picture in it, the one where something is already underway, and put that at the top. Chronology is not an obligation.

**Put the result before the process.** The finished drink, the repaired shelf, the packed box on the scale. Show what it becomes, then go back and show how it got there.

**Delete the first sentence.** Cut whatever the speaker said first, watch it again, and see whether anything is missing. Often nothing is, and the video now starts a beat later and a beat stronger. Do this before you do anything else to the timeline.

**Open mid-action or mid-sentence.** Starting a clip halfway through a movement or a phrase feels wrong while you are scrubbing and reads as urgency on a phone. Trust the phone.

## About the two seconds

Treat two seconds as a working rule of the craft, a habit that keeps you honest about how little room the opening has. It is not a measured threshold and it is not a rule any platform publishes. Nobody is going to hand you that number, and any number you are handed is worth less than the check you can run yourself: watch your own opening on your own phone, at the size a stranger sees it, and ask whether you would have stayed.

## The drill

Take any clip you already have, even a bad one. Find three frames in it that could each be the first frame. Write one sentence for each saying why a stranger would stay for it. Then choose one and recut the video so it starts there.

Run that drill three times and it changes how you watch footage. You stop looking for where the take begins and start looking for where the video begins. They are rarely the same place, and what sits between them is usually the greeting, the setup, and the breath before the point.

lessons.title: One video, one idea
lessons.content_mdx:
# One video, one idea

Openings get judged. Middles get abandoned. A viewer who stayed past the first frames leaves later for a different reason: the video stopped going anywhere, and leaving cost nothing.

A short video carries one idea. Not one topic, one idea. "Paint" is a topic. "Cheap paint costs more because you have to do three coats" is an idea, and you can tell in a single viewing whether the video delivered it.

## The promise and the payoff

The top of the video makes a promise whether or not you meant to make one. The body has to visibly move toward it. The payoff has to actually arrive.

Jomar edits for a hardware store in Imus. The owner recorded fourteen minutes about paint. Jomar's first cut opened with "cheap paint is a trap", wandered through brands, and ended with "so choose carefully". The promise was made and never paid. Somebody who watched the whole thing got nothing they could repeat to a friend, and what they learned instead is that this account does not deliver.

The open loop, where you raise a question and answer it later, is a real tool. It turns into bait the moment the answer never comes or gets pushed to a part two. Bait works once. It costs you the next video, the one that would have been watched by the person who now scrolls past your client's face.

## Write the sentence before you touch the timeline

Before importing anything, write down, on paper, the one sentence the video is making. Not the topic. The sentence.

- "Cheap paint costs more because you need three coats."
- "You can ship a fragile order for the same money if you pack it in this order."
- "This is why your rice cooker smells burnt even when the rice is fine."

Now the edit has a test. Every clip either serves that sentence or it does not, and the ones that do not come out, however good they are. This is what makes a long edit fast. You are no longer deciding what is interesting, which is a decision with no end. You are checking against something you already decided.

## Three ideas is three videos

Footage usually arrives carrying more than one idea. The instinct is to fit them all in, because the client said them all and cutting feels like throwing away work you were given.

Fit them all in and the video changes subject in the middle, which is a place to leave. Take the three ideas and make three videos instead. The client gets more, you reuse one setup, and each video is about something.

If two ideas genuinely depend on each other, they are one idea and one of them is the setup. Say the setup in a sentence and move on.

## The middle is where you lose people

Between the promise and the payoff, every second either moves toward the answer or stands still. Standing still looks like this: a second example of a point already made, a qualification nobody asked for, the speaker restating the last sentence in different words, a courtesy line about the other services the shop also offers.

Cut them. If taking a section out does not change whether the sentence lands, the section was not doing anything.

## Stop when the idea is delivered

The ending is where editors do quiet damage. The payoff lands, and then there are eleven more seconds of "so yeah, that is it, thank you for watching, see you next time".

Those seconds are the clearest exit sign in the video, and they sit exactly where you least want one. End on the payoff. If the client insists on a call to action, make it one short line that arrives with the payoff rather than trailing after it.

A last frame that resembles the first frame, the finished drink again, the packed box again, sends the viewer back up into the top of the video instead of out of it. You do not have to force this. When it fits, it is free.

## Practical

Paper, one sentence, before the timeline. Tape it to the edge of your screen where you cannot avoid reading it.

When you catch yourself defending a clip you like, read the sentence and ask what the clip does for it. If the honest answer is "nothing, but it is good", save it for the video where it is the idea.

lessons.title: Shooting for the edit
lessons.content_mdx:
# Shooting for the edit

You can only cut what somebody shot. Every editing problem that cannot be solved on the timeline was created at capture, and the fix is always the same one: get the material next time.

Trina is a VA in Davao who edits for a client in Australia. For months she received one long take per video, filmed in a bright kitchen with the electric fan on, the subject centred and standing well back. She could trim it and she could put text on it, and that was the whole of what she could do. Her videos improved the week she sent the client a shot list, not the week she learned a new app.

## Frame so you can cut later

Shoot vertical, which is the tall 9 by 16 shape a phone gives you when you hold it upright, and which is the frame this whole course assumes. That shape is stable. The things around it, the lengths a destination accepts and the file it wants, move, so look those up at the source on the day you deliver. Keep anything that has to be seen in the middle band of the frame, and confirm later, from a draft post on a phone, where the interface covers the top and bottom. The general craft of sizing and safe areas belongs to a design course, not to this one.

What is specific to a moving frame is room. Leave space around the subject while you film. That space is what lets you crop in later and build a tighter shot out of the same take, which hands you a second angle for free and a place to hide a cut. Frame somebody tight at capture and you have exactly one shot, forever.

Room costs pixels, so check what you are filming at before the shoot rather than after it. A crop is not a zoom lens. It throws away part of the picture and enlarges what is left. Film at the same size you deliver at and every punch-in comes back softer than the shots either side of it, and a viewer reads that as cheap without being able to name it. Open your camera app's settings once and film at the largest size the phone offers that still leaves you storage for the day. Then the crop is free, and not before.

Headroom is the same argument on a smaller scale. A little air above the head. Not a hand's width of ceiling, and not the top of the skull pressed against the edge of the frame.

## When the footage arrives sideways

Clients film horizontally out of habit, and the first you hear of it is when the folder opens. You have three moves and none of them is free. Crop into the middle of the horizontal frame, which loses the sides and the pixels, so it only works if the subject was centred and the file is big. Sit the horizontal shot in the middle of a vertical frame and fill the space above and below on purpose, with a title, a flat colour or a still, rather than a blurred copy of the same shot. Or ask for it again, held upright, which costs the client two minutes and is the only one of those moves that gives you a full frame. Pick one, tell the client which and why, and put "filmed upright" at the top of the shot list so the next batch does not arrive the same way.

## Coverage: five things to get every time

**A second take of the opening line.** Always. The opening carries the whole video, and the first attempt is the one where the speaker is still finding it.

**A wide and a close of the same action.** The same thing happening twice, at two distances. That is a cut you can make later without a single other clip existing.

**Ten seconds of the hands doing the thing.** Whatever the video is about, film the hands doing it, close, with nobody talking. Ten seconds of that is worth more to an editor than another minute of the face.

**Room tone.** Ten seconds of the room with nobody speaking, recorded in the same place at the same time. It sounds like nothing. It is what you lay under a gap so a cut does not thud.

**A reaction.** The face after the thing works, or the face while listening. Small, cheap, and useful in ways you cannot predict until you are cutting.

## Audio is the part you cannot fix

Get the microphone close to the person talking. A clip-on mic that plugs into the phone is the cheapest real upgrade in this craft, because it stays on the speaker's chest no matter where the phone ends up. If the client owns one, tell them to use it. If nobody owns one, move the phone in close instead. Close beats expensive every time: a cheap mic near the mouth beats a costly one across the room. What it does not beat is a microphone that is both cheap and close.

Choose the quiet room over the pretty room. The kitchen with the good window and the humming ref is worse than the bedroom with the door shut. Turn off the aircon and the fan for the take, and be uncomfortable for two minutes.

Then be honest about the limit. A voice recorded far away in a hard, echoing room was never captured clearly, and nothing puts back what the phone did not get. Tools can reduce a steady hum, and doing that leaves you with the echo. If the audio is unusable, the professional move is to ask for it again, not to bury it under music.

## Light and steadiness with no kit

Face the window. Put the person facing the light rather than with the light behind them, or you deliver a silhouette. Watch for the ceiling light directly overhead, which drops shadow into the eyes, and the one directly behind, which flares.

Brace against something. A wall, a doorframe, a stack of books, elbows planted on a table. Handheld looks fine on a phone. Unsupported handheld for a whole take does not.

## The five-minute shot list

Before anyone films anything, agree these seven lines. It fits in a phone note.

1. Filmed upright, in the tall frame.
2. The one sentence the video is making.
3. The opening line, filmed twice.
4. The main action, wide and close.
5. Ten seconds of hands.
6. Ten seconds of room tone.
7. One reaction.

Send that list to any client who films their own footage. It is the cheapest improvement available to either of you, and it costs them five minutes they were going to spend anyway.

quiz.prompt: You have forty seconds of footage of a Cebu barbershop owner explaining a fade. Four moments in it could be the first frame. Which one do you cut to the top?

options.text: The shop sign and the open door, held for a beat so the viewer knows where this is.
The owner mid-cut, clippers already moving, with the shape of the fade half finished.
The empty chair with the tools laid out neatly, before anybody has sat down in it.
The owner seated and smiling at the camera, taking a breath before he greets people.

quiz.explanation: The first frame has to have something already happening in it. The sign, the empty chair and the breath before the greeting are all setup, and setup is what a thumb scrolls past. Starting mid-cut puts the subject, the movement and the topic on screen in the same instant.

quiz.prompt: Your rough cut for a Marikina shoe repair shop opens with the owner saying, "So in this video I will be explaining the difference between a resole and a full rebuild." The rest of the video is strong. What is the best fix?

options.text: Keep the line and lay fast music under it so the opening has energy while he sets up.
Keep the line but put a text hook over it so there is something to read while he talks.
Cut the line and open on his hands peeling the old sole off, and let his voice come in over it.
Swap the line for a short friendly greeting so the video still feels warm before the work starts.

quiz.explanation: That sentence is a table of contents, and nobody came for one. Deleting the first line and checking whether anything is missing is the fastest test in this craft. Here nothing is missing: the hands pulling the old sole away say what the video is about, faster and without asking anyone to wait.

quiz.prompt: A client sends one take where she explains why her ube jam keeps without preservatives, then, in the same take, runs through her delivery cut-off times. She wants one video. How do you cut it?

options.text: Build the video on the preservatives idea alone, and make the delivery cut-offs a second one.
Cut both in, with a text card between them so the change of subject is at least signposted.
Keep the delivery cut-offs and drop the preservatives, since the practical part is more useful.
Trim both hard so each one gets an equal share and the whole thing still comes out short.

quiz.explanation: Two ideas in one short video means the video changes subject in the middle, and a change of subject is a place to leave. Signposting it does not fix that. The client is not losing anything either: she gets two videos out of one setup, and each one is about something a viewer can repeat.

quiz.prompt: You are filming a testimonial on a phone and you already know you will want a tighter shot partway through the take. What do you do while the camera is rolling?

options.text: Frame the subject tight now, so the footage already looks close and needs no extra work later.
Use the phone's zoom halfway through the take so the change of shot is captured live.
Shoot the whole take wide and plan to add movement to the shot during the edit instead.
Leave room around the subject so that a later crop still holds them properly in the frame.

quiz.explanation: Room around the subject is what lets you crop in later and get a second angle out of one take. Framed tight at capture, you have one shot forever. Zooming live commits you to the change at a moment you cannot revise, and a wide take of empty space is not a shot you can rescue with movement.

quiz.prompt: Arvin filmed alone and got exactly one take of the opening line, which he fumbled. He is filming the next video this afternoon. What goes on the shot list?

options.text: A written script taped next to the phone so the line comes out right on the first attempt.
A full second run of the entire video, so there is a complete backup of everything he says on camera.
A wide version of the whole take, to cut to whenever the close version has a stumble in it.
A second take of the opening line, recorded straight after the first one, on every single shoot.

quiz.explanation: The opening carries the video and the first attempt is the one where the speaker is still finding it, so a second take of that one line is the cheapest insurance on the list. A script does not stop a fumble, a wide alternative still carries the fumbled words, and reshooting everything is how filming stops happening at all.

quiz.prompt: Lorna has twelve minutes of client footage from a plant shop in Marilao and one afternoon to cut it. What does she do before she opens the timeline?

options.text: Watch all twelve minutes and mark every usable moment so nothing good gets missed later.
Write down the one sentence the video is making, then cut only what serves that sentence.
Import everything and start trimming from the top, deciding what stays as she goes along.
Find the strongest thirty seconds in the footage and build the video around what is in it.

quiz.explanation: Written down first, the sentence turns every later decision into a check rather than a judgement call, which is what makes a long edit fast. Marking everything usable and building around the best clip both leave her deciding what is interesting, and that decision has no end.

quiz.prompt: You are filming a demo where on-screen text will sit under the subject for the whole video. The client asks where she should leave space. What do you tell her?

options.text: Leave the top and bottom thirds empty and shoot everything through the middle strip, so the placement never needs checking.
Fill the frame with the subject, then move the text wherever there is space during the edit and check it on a phone at the end.
Keep the subject in the middle band of the frame, and confirm the placement later from a draft post on a real phone.
Shoot it wide so there is empty space all around the subject, then place the text after the video is exported.

quiz.explanation: The area an interface covers is not a number anybody can tell you once. It differs between apps and it changes without notice, so a stated fraction of the frame is a guess wearing the clothes of a spec, and hollowing the frame out to a middle strip throws away the picture to buy a guarantee nobody can give. Keep what matters in the middle band, then look at the video from a draft post on a phone. A file sitting in a camera roll shows you the frame, not what the app puts on top of it.

quiz.prompt: Client footage arrives shot in a bright tiled kitchen, the subject standing well back from the phone, with aircon hum on every take. What do you tell the client?

options.text: Ask for the takes again, in a smaller room, with the aircon off and the phone held close to her.
Accept it and clean the hum up in the edit, since a steady noise is the kind of thing tools handle.
Accept it and run music across the whole video so the hum sits underneath the track.
Ask for one clean take of the opening line only, and keep the rest of the footage as it is.

quiz.explanation: A voice recorded far away in a hard room was never captured clearly, and no tool puts back what the phone did not get. Pulling the hum out leaves you with the echo. Music and text cover the symptom while the viewer still hears a thin, distant voice, and that is the thing that makes them leave. Refilming only the opening line leaves the same problem running through every sentence after it.
